_shape: Tickets that block each other. Launched in waves by dependency, merged blockers first.
_why_this_works: parallel-tickets is the better shape and has no integration step at all. Use it whenever the tickets are independent. This shape is for the case it refuses: tickets whose blocking edges are real. The edges do the scheduling, so every member starts against code its blockers already finished.
_input: Tickets, not a spec and not a plan. Each ticket is a thin vertical slice that names the tickets that block it. Given a spec or a bare conversation instead, stop and ask the user to write tickets first.
_rules: Read every ticket IN FULL before scheduling. Titles and blocking edges alone will mis-schedule the waves.

Write each brief with three sections: 'Done when' (acceptance criteria you can check), 'Out of scope', and 'When to do nothing' (the preconditions under which the member changes nothing and reports why). State the end state, not the steps.
Work out each ticket's file ownership by reading the codebase, never by paraphrasing the ticket. That footprint goes in the brief under 'Files you own' and is the hard boundary.
Wave 1 is every ticket whose blockers are all done. Cap a wave at five members. More than that and the lead spends its whole context on reports.
Two tickets in one wave that touch the same files go in DIFFERENT waves. Worktrees remove the write race, not the merge conflict.
Settle open questions before wave 1. Every question you answer yourself later becomes a guess made in several fresh contexts at once.
Run one wave at a time. Let a wave finish, then recompute what is unblocked. A member that finished may have changed what its dependents need.
Later waves join the SAME team with `teamwire launch --add` and new role names. One team, one archive, one report path. Never run wave 1 and wave 2 as separate teams.

A dependent member's base is its blocker's branch, not main, so it starts on the code it depends on. Launch it only after the blocker reported and `teamwire verify` passed. Merge blockers first, so each merge lands on the code it was written against.
On the merged result run the full gate once and review the whole change. Each member reviewed its own slice alone, so the merge is still unreviewed.

Give every implementer a "check" (the targeted command that proves its work, which you run once first) and an "owns" list. `teamwire verify <team>` runs every check itself and flags edits outside owns, deleted or skipped tests and changed check configuration. It is the step before any merge; a member's done report is a claim.
PILOT FIRST from about four members up. Launch ONE member, read its result, run `teamwire verify <team>` on it, fix the brief, then add the rest.

One coherent change per branch. A ticket that touches more than one module is two members, or one member with two units. Size each task by its reference fix: in SWE-bench Live, a task whose fix was one file under five lines was solved 48% of the time, and one needing three or more files or over 100 lines under 10%. Devin does best on "clear, upfront requirements and verifiable outcomes that would take a junior engineer 4-8 hrs of work". Anthropic's agent-teams docs advise 3-5 teammates with 5-6 tasks each (items on a teammate's shared task list, not units in one brief).
